activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: When a variable appears on both sides, as in 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, subtracting 3x from both sides gathers the variable on one side: 2x + 2 = 10.
story:
Benjamin had promised his mother he would pass the retest on Friday, which was why he was sitting in the community centre tutoring room on a Tuesday afternoon, staring at 5x + 2 = 3x + 10 like it had personally insulted him. Around him the room hummed with pencils and low voices. Kylee was two tables over, and Gibson sat beside him, tapping his own worksheet.

"I don't get it," Benjamin said. "There's an x on both sides. Which one do I move?"

Gibson shrugged. "Mine's worse. Mine has fractions."

Mr. Ivanova, who ran the tutoring centre, drifted past their table. He didn't stop or lecture; he just said, "Try one and see what happens," and kept walking toward the coffee machine.

Benjamin thought about last month, when he'd guessed on the whole quiz and gotten a 41. Guessing had felt fast and easy right up until it wasn't. Maybe that was the real mistake, not the algebra itself. He decided to test an idea instead of guessing. He would subtract 3x from both sides and watch what happened.

On the left side, 5x take away 3x left 2x, so the left became 2x + 2. On the right, 3x take away 3x left nothing, so the right became just 10. He sat back. The equation was 2x + 2 = 10 now, with all the x's gathered on one side, and that he could solve. Two from both sides, then divide both sides by two. x = 4. He checked it by plugging it back into the original: 5 times 4 plus 2 was 22, and 3 times 4 plus 10 was also 22. It worked.

"Kylee," he called across the aisle, "try subtracting the x from one side off both sides. Like this one, 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, I took away 3x from both sides and got 2x + 2 = 10."

Kylee tried it her way, subtracting 5x from both sides instead, and got negative 2x plus 2 equals negative 2x plus... she frowned, crossed out, and tried again. Either way worked, she announced, you just had to be careful with your signs.

Benjamin felt something he could only call optimistic for the first time all week. He wondered whether Mr. Ivanova had known that "try one and see" would work better than an explanation. Probably. That seemed like the kind of thing a person learned from years of watching kids give up.

Before they left, Gibson offered him half a granola bar in exchange for help with the fractions, and Benjamin agreed, though he felt a small pang about doing Gibson's thinking for him. He would compromise: he'd show the first step and let Gibson do the rest. Empathy, his mother called it, when you remembered what struggling felt like. He slid his worksheet across so Gibson could see the x's lined up neatly on one side.

"First step's yours," Benjamin said, and tapped the page.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, the sentence ends with a comma inside the quotation marks instead of a period, as in "I'm ready," she said.
story:
Gabriella sat cross-legged on her grandmother's porch with her notebook balanced on her knees, because in exactly two days, Ms. Halvorsen's writing club would meet, and everyone had to read a finished story out loud. Her grandmother had already promised a plate of lemon bars for the meeting, since the club was being held right there in the living room. The only problem was the story itself. Gabriella had a climber stuck on a cliff, a storm rolling in, and no idea how to end it, and every time she wrote a line of talking, it looked wrong on the page.

Parker arrived on his bike at noon, skidding up the gravel drive with a red pen tucked behind his ear like a carpenter's pencil. He had volunteered to mark her draft, which had seemed like a great idea right up until he started circling things. "Here," he said, tapping the page. "'The ledge is crumbling.' Period. Then 'she said.' You can't have a period there. It's wrong every single time it happens, and it happens, like, eleven times."

"But it's a sentence," Gabriella said, snatching the notebook back. "'The ledge is crumbling.' That's a whole sentence. Sentences end in periods. That's the rule of the universe." Parker just shook his head and pointed at the page again, and Gabriella noticed something odd. Every circle he had drawn sat around a period that came right before she said or he yelled. When the tag came first, like when she wrote, Ariya whispered, "Don't look down," the period lived happily inside the quotation marks and Parker had circled nothing at all. There was a pattern, and patterns meant a rule, and rules meant she could test it.

She flipped to a fresh page and wrote three versions of the same line. In the first, the tag came after the speech with a period, and Parker circled it. In the second, she swapped the period for a comma, still tucked inside the quotation marks, and Parker's pen hovered and then dropped. "That one's fine," he said, sounding almost disappointed. "Why is that fine?" "No idea," Gabriella said, her heart thumping. "But it's fine every time." She wrote five more lines, each one ending with a comma inside the quotation marks before the tag, and Parker circled none of them. When the tag followed a spoken sentence, the comma took the period's place, every single time, like a substitute player who always showed up.

"Do you think I'm gullible?" Parker asked, squinting at her. "Because if you made these up to mess with me, that's cold." "They're real," Gabriella said. "I tested them on paper. That's science." Her grandmother came out with lemonade and peered at the circles. "In my day we called that punctuation, and we feared it," she said, and went back inside.

Gabriella worked until dark, and her stamina outlasted Parker's, who kept insisting the cliff scene was too scary to fix. She rewrote every line of dialogue with the comma inside the quotation marks, and then she solved the climax too: the climber's ledge would erode, crumb by crumb, until she had to jump for the rope her partner had anchored above, and the last spoken line would be, "Jump now," Marco shouted. She underlined it twice.

On club day, Ariya leaned over the notebook before Gabriella's turn. "Is that a cliff story?" "With a rope and a storm and a ledge that falls apart," Gabriella said, and stood up. "The ledge is crumbling," she said.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Alexis flattened the crumpled note against her desk and read it again, even though she already knew it by heart. "Can't come to the sleepover. Sorry." That was all Lauriane had written, and all Alexis had gotten in three days. She slid it under her math book so she wouldn't have to look at it, then pulled it back out. Some best friend, she thought. Lauriane was just selfish, plain and simple, the kind of person who bails the second something better comes along.

At the front of the room, Mr. Kaya was writing an equation on the board, and Alexis copied it without really seeing it. Beside her, Bo leaned over. "You and Lauriane still not talking?" he whispered.

"She ditched me. Why would I talk to her?"

Bo shrugged. "Weird, though. She loves your sleepovers. Last time she brought that sparkly pillow and wouldn't let anyone touch it." He tapped his pencil. "People don't usually ditch stuff they love for no reason."

Alexis turned that over while Mr. Kaya's markers squeaked against the board. Something was off, like a math problem where the answer came out wrong and you knew you'd missed a step somewhere. Lauriane had been planning this sleepover for two weeks. Something had to be jamming the works, something Alexis couldn't see from where she sat. She tested the idea the only way she could: she wrote a note during silent reading, pressing hard enough to submerge the pencil tip into the soft pink eraser at the end.

"Are you mad at me?" she wrote. "Please tell me what happened."

At lunch, Lauriane found her by the window, and the answer came out in a rush. "My grandma had a heart attack Friday night. We drove to the hospital and I sat in the waiting room until two in the morning. I couldn't even think about writing a real note. I'm sorry."

Alexis's stomach dropped. She had decided Lauriane was selfish, and she had been completely wrong. Later, in social studies, Mr. Kaya mentioned that people blame behavior on character and overlook the situation, and Alexis nearly dropped her pencil.

"It's called the fundamental attribution error," Mr. Kaya said. "Named by a psychologist, Lee Ross, in 1977."

"That's what I did," Alexis whispered to Bo. "I thought she was just selfish because of who she is, and I never even thought about what was happening to her."

Bo nodded. "Seemed that way."

That afternoon, Alexis wrote one more note, the paper smelling faintly of lavender because Lauriane's sister had spilled soap in her backpack. "How is your grandma? Want to come Friday instead? I'll save the sparkly pillow spot."

At the last bell, Lauriane caught her in the hallway, note in hand, and smiled for the first time all week. "She's okay. And I'm bringing the pillow."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
Gabrielle's new phone arrived on a Tuesday, in a box so thin she couldn't believe a whole screen fit inside. She carried it to school cupped in both hands like a small, sleeping animal. At lunch, Emaan leaned across the table to look, and Zayden asked, "Does it have night mode?"

"Obviously," said Gabrielle, though she hadn't checked yet. That night she found it, a setting that made the screen glow warm and orange instead of blue-white. Perfect, she thought. She could watch videos in bed, relaxed and cozy, and drift right off.

She did not drift right off. She lay in the dark for what felt like an hour, listening to the house tick and settle. The same thing happened Wednesday, and Thursday, and by Friday she was dragging herself through Mr. Joshi's science class like her shoes were full of sand.

"You look terrible," Emaan whispered.

"Thanks." Gabrielle rubbed her eyes. "I keep scrolling a little before bed, and then I just lie there awake. My brain won't shut the door."

Emaan frowned. "My cousin had that. She kept her phone on all night and couldn't sleep either. Her doctor said something about melatonin."

"Melatonin?" Gabrielle had never heard the word. "What's that?"

"The hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening," Emaan said. "Screen light can slow it down. Blue light especially."

Gabrielle sat up so fast her stool squeaked. A theory was forming, the kind Mr. Joshi loved: something invisible, a hidden cause, like guessing which wire made the buzzer sound in a circuit. Maybe the phone wasn't just keeping her awake because it was interesting. Maybe the light itself was doing something, holding back the very thing that made her sleepy. And wasn't she most vulnerable to that at night, alone in the dark with the screen an inch from her face?

She decided to test it the way a scientist would, one change at a time. Friday night she put the phone on the dresser, far from the bed, and read a paper book until her eyes felt heavy. She fell asleep so fast she barely remembered turning off the lamp. Saturday night she let herself scroll in bed again, just to be sure, and lay awake watching the ceiling. That was the twist, and it landed hard: the phone she'd been so desperate to keep in her hand at night was the exact thing ruining her nights. She'd thought the videos relaxed her. Now the evidence said otherwise.

On Monday, Zayden tried to petition her at lunch. "Come on, just one video tonight, we can send stuff back and forth."

"Nope," said Gabrielle. "Phone goes on the dresser at nine. Book until I'm sleepy." She grinned. "Turns out my phone is great. It just can't be my nightlight."

Emaan raised her milk carton like a toast. "To melatonin."

"To melatonin," said Gabrielle, and clinked her carton against it.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Antoine spread the four drama-camp games across his bedroom floor like a card dealer who had no idea what he was doing. His best audience was in the kitchen, though, and he knew it. "Raylan! Jakub! Bring the popcorn and get in here."

They came, because at Antoine's house there was always popcorn and the smell of melted butter, a small commerce of snacks that his mom ran without ever asking for payment. Raylan bounced onto the bed immediately. He wanted one thing from every scene they'd tried at camp this week: to be the funny one. So far he'd gotten laughs by ruining everything.

"Okay, new game," Antoine said. "We do a two-person scene, and whatever the other person says, you have to say yes, and then add something. Ms. Tremblay says that's the whole secret."

"That's it?" Raylan asked. "That sounds easy."

"You said that yesterday, and then you shot down every single thing I offered." Antoine had been turning that over all night. Was Raylan blocking him on purpose, or was something else going on? He had a guess: Raylan thought that agreeing made him boring, and only surprises were funny. Antoine wanted to test it. "This time, you can't say no, can't ask a question, can't change the subject. Deal?"

"Deal," Raylan said, already grinning.

Jakub flipped through the worn book Antoine had carried home from camp, the one the counselor kept in her back pocket. "Look at this. Viola Spolin, 1963, Improvisation for the Theater. The counselor says people call it the bible of improv teaching."

"So it's old and everybody still uses it," Antoine said. "There must be something in it." He felt oddly buoyant, like the book was proof the game had rules, and rules could be learned.

"Scene," Jakub announced. "Antoine, you're a pilot. Raylan, you're the passenger."

Antoine turned a chair backward and straddled it. "Welcome aboard, we're flying to the moon today."

"Yes, and," Raylan said, and Antoine watched him physically fight the urge, "I brought my own helmet, because last time the co-pilot flew with his head out the window." He lifted the popcorn bowl onto his head.

They were both laughing before the scene ended, and here was the strange part Antoine noticed: Raylan was funnier when he agreed than when he'd blocked. "Wait," Antoine said. "Do you get it? When you said yes, I gave you something better to be funny with. When you blocked me, I had nothing."

Raylan tilted the popcorn bowl off his head and thought about it. "So if I want the best jokes, I have to prioritize your idea first?"

"Try it," Antoine said, and turned the chair around again. "Welcome aboard. This time we're diving to the bottom of the ocean."

"Yes, and," Raylan said, "I brought seventeen sandwiches, because sharks get hungry too."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
Brielle noticed it first at the picnic table by the swings, where the whole soccer team was supposed to be celebrating. Ines was stacking paper cups instead of eating her cake, and Elijah kept checking the roster on his phone even though the season was over. Nobody looked sad exactly, but nobody looked like a party either. "It's like everyone's half here," Brielle said to Ines. "We won our last game Saturday. This should be the fun part."

That afternoon, Brielle had found something in her cousin's old psychology textbook, left behind on the porch. It said groups move through stages, forming and storming and a few others, and that in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, called adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. She had almost skipped that page. Now she wondered if it fit.

She decided to test it. At the next table, Ms. Oyelaran, who coached the park league, was folding the team banner, so Brielle wandered over and asked an easy question. "Do teams usually feel weird at the end of the season, even when they won?" The coach laughed a little. "Every single year. Even my college team, and that was a while ago." So it was a pattern, not just her friends being strange.

Her second test was trickier. If the feeling came from the group breaking up, then anything that kept the group real should push against it. She went back to the table and said, "Next year some of us will integrate with the new players, and we'll have to build a whole new team." Elijah looked up from his phone. "That's the weird part. We're already talking about a team that doesn't exist yet." Ines stopped stacking cups. "So we're all feeling the same thing," she said slowly. "I thought it was just me being ridiculous."

"It has a name," Brielle said. "Adjourning." She spread the last four slices of cake so everyone got one, including the twins who always sat at the far end. Ms. Oyelaran brought the banner over, and they all signed the corner of it in marker, Elijah writing his name enormous across the middle. Then Ines stood and cupped her hands around her mouth. "Same park, same table, first Saturday of summer," she called. "Even if we're on different teams, even if we're just civilians in regular clothes."

Brielle folded her napkin into a small triangle, like a corner flag, and planted it upright in the middle of her cake.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
story:
Amelia crouched beside the trail with a pair of tweezers, peeling a paper-thin layer from the inside of a wild onion her dad had pulled from the garden that morning. She carried the peel in a folded page of her notebook up the gravel path to the picnic table where Mr. Gupta's field science club met on Saturdays. Today's task was written on the whiteboard he hauled out in his wagon: prepare a slide, find the cells, and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Whoever finished first got to put their drawing up in the school hallway. Amelia wanted that spot on the wall more than she had wanted anything since she'd missed the honor roll by two points in October.

Cordelia was already at the table, twisting the fine focus knob on the club's little portable microscope. "I can see squares," she said, "but that's all. Just squares, like a window with no glass." She wanted the hallway spot too, and she was faster with a pencil, which everyone knew. Amelia laid her onion skin flat on a slide, added a drop of water, and lowered the cover slip the way the instruction sheet showed, at an angle so no bubbles would sneak underneath.

She pressed her eye to the eyepiece and turned the knob. Squares, exactly as Cordelia had said, running in parallel rows like bricks in a garden wall, and so faint they seemed made of fog. The cell walls were barely there, the membrane invisible, and nowhere at all could she find a nucleus. She sat back, jaw tight. A labeled drawing needed three things, and she could see one, and only just. She started to wonder whether her peel was too thick, or too thin, or whether she had wasted her whole Saturday.

Then she thought about it differently. The cells had to be there, whole and complete, whether she could see them or not. The problem might not be the peel. It might be that the cells were nearly colourless, and her eye needed something to push against. She remembered the small brown bottle in Mr. Gupta's supply box, the one nobody had touched yet, and a note her friend Marianna had tucked into her backpack that morning: "Amelia, my brother did this lab last year. He says the blank slide is the trap. Look in the box for the amber bottle. Don't ask Cordelia. Race you to the wall." Amelia had laughed at the time. Now she read it again, twice.

She fetched the bottle. The label said iodine. She lifted the cover slip, put one drop of stain onto the onion skin, and set the glass back down. Cordelia looked over, frowning. "What did you do that for?"

"Watch," Amelia said. She leaned in, turned the knob, and there it was: the walls standing out sharp and dark, and inside each cell a small round nucleus, deep amber, unmistakable. She found the membrane along the inner edge of each wall and started her drawing, lettering the three labels in her neatest hand. Cordelia grabbed the iodine next, muttering that Marianna had better not have written to Amelia too.

By four o'clock two drawings hung in the hallway side by side. Marianna walked past, looked at both, and grinned. "Next time," she told Cordelia, "read your own mail."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
The trouble started every Tuesday, right before fourth period. Aiden's stomach knotted, his hands went cold, and he could not stop imagining the moment Mr. Ross would call him to the front for his current events talk. He had begun to wonder if something was wrong with him, so he did what he always did with puzzles: he gathered evidence. He kept a folded page in his binder, and each time the sick feeling came, he wrote down where he was and what was about to happen. After two weeks the pattern was clear. It was never before lunch, never before gym, only before he had to speak in front of the class.

"You look like you're bracing for a punch," Alexy said on the way to class, which was Alexy's way of saying he was worried without actually saying it.

"It's presentation day again," Aiden said. He showed Alexy the folded page, because Alexy was good at spotting things Aiden missed. "I think it's the talking in front of people. I never get this way before a math quiz, even a hard one."

Alexy studied the page like it was a score sheet. "Then maybe stop trying to be the conventional presenter, you know, standing up there all stiff like a news anchor. Maybe that would help." Alexy wanted the two of them to enter the school invention fair together, and he had said more than once that he needed Aiden at his best. "I need my partner, not a statue."

In fourth period, Aiden tried the idea out as a small experiment. Instead of gripping the note cards, he set them on the podium and told the class, honestly, that presentations stressed him out and that his coping plan was to take one slow breath before each new slide. A few kids nodded. His stomach still fluttered, but it did not take over. Afterward, Kianna caught up with him in the hallway.

"Can I tell you something?" she said. "I used to hide in the bathroom before every choir solo. My mom took me to the doctor, and the doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but mine was so intense and it lasted so long and it got in the way of everyday stuff, so she diagnosed an anxiety disorder." She shrugged. "It's treatable. I've got ways of handling it now, and it got a lot better."

"Treatable," Aiden repeated, writing the word on his folded page right under his Tuesday notes. A wave of guilt passed through him, remembering the week he had snapped at his little brother for no reason other than the knotted stomach. This was bigger than note cards, maybe, but it had a shape now, and shapes could be handled.

"We should tell Mr. Ross," Kianna said. "Not for a big speech. Just so he knows presentations are hard for some of us. I can set that boundary, you can back me up."

Aiden closed his notebook and followed her toward the classroom door.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Lucas stood in his grandfather's hallway with the paper shaking slightly in his hand. In three days he would read the blessing at his bar mitzvah, in Hebrew, in front of two hundred people, and he could not get past the fourth line. He had tried repeating it out loud, writing it ten times, even recording it and playing it under his pillow, but the words scattered like they were random noise in his head.

He wandered into the kitchen, where his grandfather was tightening a screw under the sink. "I keep forgetting the middle part," Lucas said. "It just disappears."

His grandfather dried his hands and looked at him for a moment. "You know, when I was your age, I learned my portion the old way. The method of loci. You link each part of the text to a place along a familiar route, then you walk that route in your mind to recall it."

"Walk it in my mind?"

"Try it and see." His grandfather picked up his toolbox. "This house is your route. You've walked it ten thousand times."

So Lucas began. He put the first line in the front hall, right on the hook where his grandfather's cap always hung. The second line went in the kitchen, sitting on the counter beside the breadbox. He imagined the third line squeezed into the cupboard with the chipped blue mugs, and the fourth line, the one that kept vanishing, he installed firmly on the middle shelf of the living room bookcase, leaning against the dictionary like a bookmark. Line by line he filled the house, all the way up the stairs to the bathroom mirror, where the final words hung like steam on the glass.

That night he lay in bed and tested it. He closed his eyes and walked from the front door through every room, and the lines were there, waiting on their hooks and shelves exactly where he had left them. When he reached the bathroom mirror, he said the last words out loud into the dark, and they came out whole.

The next morning Kathleen came over to quiz him. She sat at the kitchen table with the paper folded in her lap while he paced the hallway with his eyes shut, and when he finished without a single stumble she looked up at him with her mouth open.

"How?" she said.

Lucas grinned and tapped the wall beside the cap hook. "Line one lives right there."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
story:
Aaron pulled the jar of chicken soup from the back of the refrigerator and nearly dropped it. The lid had bulged upward like a small hill, and when he twisted it, a sour smell leaked out. Beside it sat a sealed can of the same soup, perfectly fine. He set both on the counter and frowned. Same soup, same fridge, same two weeks. Why had one gone bad?

He called Lyndon, who biked over with Alexe trailing behind on a scooter. "Okay," Lyndon said, peering at the jar, "so what's your hypothesis? You keep using that word for the science fair."

"It's a testable guess," Aaron said. "You don't just wonder, you set it up so the answer can prove you wrong." His first hypothesis was that sealed containers kept food good, but the bulging lid made him pause. Something invisible had been at work inside the jar, alive enough to puff the lid up. That was the hidden cause he wanted to catch.

Alexe slid the soup can across the counter. "This is basically the equivalent of your jar, right? Same soup, different container." Aaron nodded slowly, then got out two clean jars and a pot. He boiled fresh broth in both, then capped one jar tight right away and left the other open on the counter, half covered, so only things floating in the air could get in.

Mr. Le, their neighbour, was retrieving his newspaper when Alexe waved him over to the door. "Do you know much about spoiled soup?" she asked.

"One thing," Mr. Le said. "Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck." He tapped the doorframe. "Famous experiment. You could look it up." Then he went back to his newspaper.

Aaron wrote that down and stared at it. If germs drifted in on dust, an open jar should go bad and a sealed one should not, and the bend of a neck could stop the dust without stopping the air. His open jar, three days later, smelled like the first one. The sealed jar stayed clear. "It works," he said, "my hypothesis survived the test."

For the fair, he tried to quantify it by counting the cloudy patches in each jar and making a chart. "Each patch is probably a whole colony," Lyndon said, "like the descendant of one germ that landed."

On the morning of the fair, Aaron packed the jars in a shoebox with the chart on top, along with a glass tube he'd bent into an S shape over the stove with his mom's help. He set the box by the door and picked up the tube, holding it up to the window light.

"Best guess in the world," he said, "and now we find out if it holds."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, and a person's karma, the results of their actions, shapes their next life.
story:
John spread his homework across the kitchen table: a worksheet titled "Big Questions, Different Answers," a pencil chewed at both ends, and two plates of toast because research made him hungry. The assignment asked him to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and he had picked Christianity, because his grandma had explained heaven to him about a thousand times, and Hinduism, because his best friend Myles was Hindu and Myles knew everything about everything and said so.

His notes on the Christian side filled half a page. On the Hindu side he had written exactly one word: "ask Myles." That was sparse, even by his standards. He texted, and ten minutes later Myles let himself in through the back door like he lived there, which he basically did.

"You can't just write ask Myles," Myles said, reading over his shoulder while stealing the second piece of toast. "That violates like three rules of homework."

"It violates zero rules. It's a plan. Plans are allowed." John pulled out a fresh sheet. "Okay. Tell me the whole thing, slowly, I'm writing it down."

"So in Hinduism, the soul goes through samsara," Myles said. "That's the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. And your karma decides what your next life is like. Karma is the results of your actions."

John wrote it all down, then frowned at his paper. "Wait. So nobody just... stops and goes somewhere and stays?"

"Nope. You come back. Over and over."

"So heaven is like the last stop on the train, and samsara is like being on a carousel that keeps giving you new horses."

Myles chewed his toast. "That's actually not bad. Steal it. Put it in your homework."

John stared at the two pages, tapping his pencil, then sat up so fast he knocked the empty plate onto the floor. "Oh no. Oh no. I've been testing this my whole life without knowing it."

"Testing what?"

"The karma thing. The results of your actions. Last week I fed your little sister's hamster the wrong food and it got a stomachache. And then on Saturday I fell off my bike into Mr. Dang's hedge. And then yesterday I lost my retainer. Three bad things. Three bad actions. That's a formula, Myles. My karma is tracking me."

"You fed Oreo a grape?" Myles was laughing so hard he had to hold the table. "Grapes are poison for hamsters, you absolute turnip. That's not karma, that's just cause and effect with witnesses."

"Same thing," John said stubbornly. "Actions, results. I'm just saying the system is working faster than anyone told me."

He copied both columns neatly, and at the bottom he wrote his conclusion: nobody can see past death, so every faith is a theory about the part nobody came back to describe, and the hamster was fine, so possibly he still had time to improve his numbers. Then he leaned across the table and pointed his pencil at Myles.

"Just so you know, if I come back as anything with homework, I'm blaming you."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
Grayson flopped onto the bench beside Annabelle and peeled off his skates, wincing when his left thigh twinged. "You okay?" Annabelle asked, already handing him his water bottle before he could answer. He nodded, but by the time Tuesday practice rolled around, both his legs ached so badly that climbing the rink steps felt like a punishment.

"It's the lactic acid," said one of the defensemen in the locker room, rubbing his calves. "Coach said it builds up when you skate hard. That's why we're all sore today." Grayson frowned. Something about that didn't line up. Practice had ended Monday afternoon, more than twenty-four hours ago. If something had built up during practice, why would it wait a whole day to hurt? He skated anyway, diligent about every drill, though his legs burned on the crossovers.

That night he looked it up on the library computer while waiting for his mom to pick him up. He found that lactic acid goes back to normal levels within about an hour after exercise. An hour. So the soreness that showed up the next day couldn't be from lactic acid at all. He read the sentence twice, then copied it onto the back of his glove tag with a pencil stub, because it seemed like the kind of thing a whole team might want to know.

At Thursday practice, the defenseman was limping again and blaming the same culprit. "Lactic acid, man. It's the worst." Grayson skated over. "I looked it up," he said. "Lactic acid returns to normal within about an hour after exercise. So it can't be what's making us sore a day later. It's something else, I guess. The delayed stuff." The defenseman stared at him. "Then what is it?" "I don't know yet," Grayson admitted. "But at least now we know what it isn't."

Annabelle, who had been eavesdropping from the boards, skated a slow circle around them. "So we need a new theory," she said. Grayson decided to test one. He split his water bottle time evenly through practice on Saturday instead of gulping it all at the end, and he stretched for five full minutes afterward while everyone else bolted for the parking lot. When Sunday came, his legs still ached, but only about half as much. One trial wasn't proof, and he knew it, but it gave him something to evaluate. He wrote the result on the glove tag too.

On Monday he found Lilianne sitting alone at the far end of the bench, massaging her hamstrings and pretending not to. She was the youngest player on the team and hated looking slow. Grayson sat down, held out the glove tag, and said, "Read this. Then try what I did on Saturday." Lilianne squinted at the penciled words, then at him.

"An hour?" she said.

"An hour," Grayson said, and pointed at the stretch mats by the vending machine.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: Two things happening together, a correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; a third factor may cause both.
story:
The cafeteria at Northgate Middle School smelled like burnt coffee and floor wax, and Olivia spread her debate notes across a wobbly table beside the vending machines. Her first round started in twenty minutes, and her case still had a hole in it the size of the one Saanvi kept poking at.

"You're just listing facts," Saanvi said, tapping the page with a pen. "You say summer heat, and then you say drownings go up. So what?"

Olivia stared at her own handwriting. Round one was against a school that had beaten their team twice, and Ms. Flores had told them last practice that judges wanted points built like a bridge, each one crossing from start to finish. Olivia had copied the words claim, evidence, and warrant onto her notepad, but she still wasn't sure how to make them hold weight.

Then she heard the team at the next table rehearsing. A tall boy was delivering his argument in a clear, confident voice: ice cream sales and sunburn cases both climb every summer, therefore ice cream causes sunburn. His partner nodded along, pleased with it, and the whole thing sounded convincing until Olivia actually pictured it. Both numbers rising together didn't mean one pushed the other. She thought of her own summer: more ice cream, more sunburn, and underneath both of them the sun itself, hotter days making everyone buy cones and making everyone burn. Something third could be driving the pair, hiding below like a current under still water.

She scribbled on her notepad and turned to Saanvi. "That's the flaw in their whole case. It's a correlation, and that doesn't prove one thing causes the other. A third factor can cause both." She wrote it in the margin of her rebuttal sheet, then rebuilt her own case the same way: claim, then evidence, then the warrant, the bridge explaining why her evidence actually supported her claim instead of just sitting beside it. Ania wandered over with a bag of chips and read the margin upside down.

"That's good," Ania said. "Now regulate how fast you talk, or the judge won't catch any of it." Olivia practiced the rebuttal once, slow and steady, like reading a stanza of a poem aloud, pausing where the pauses belonged. The timer buzzed, and they walked down the hallway to Room 114, where the tall boy was already arranging his podium.

When he delivered his ice cream argument, Olivia stood, flipped to her margin, and asked the judge what season both numbers rose in, and what else rose with it. The boy flipped through his cards and found nothing written there. At the end of the round, the judge circled a note on the ballot and said the debate turned on a single question the affirmative never answered. Outside in the hallway, Saanvi hugged her notepad and laughed.

"Seventeen minutes of prep, and it came down to one line about summer."

"Next time I'm picking a less arbitrary topic," Olivia said, and folded the margin note into her pocket.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
The gallery on Miller Street had a whole wall of paintings showing city streets, and Ruby had come with her sketchbook because Ms. Hussain had promised a prize for whoever submitted the best street drawing by Friday. Ruby could draw horses and hands and bowls of fruit, but streets kept coming out flat, like stage sets pushed together with no room behind them. She stood in front of a painting called "Fifth Avenue" and copied a lamppost, then a doorway, then gave up and ate half her granola bar.

Israel and Ryder found her on the bench by the window. "You look like your drawing bit you," Israel said. He leaned over her sketchbook. Three lampposts stood in a row, all the same height, all the same distance apart, like fence posts.

"The painting does something mine doesn't," Ruby said. She pointed at the canvas. In the painting, the lampposts shrank as they went away, and the buildings leaned toward each other. Ryder squinted and held his pencil up against the canvas, tilting it to follow the roofline of one building.

"They all go to the same spot," he said. "Look, the curb, the roof, the windows, everything runs down to that door in the middle." Ruby traced the lines with her finger. Every edge she checked slid toward one point, a small dark doorway far down the street, and stopped there. The word came back to her from a video she'd half watched: vanishing point.

At home that evening she searched her dad's art book and found a diagram. One-point perspective, it said, worked when you faced straight down a street, so the fronts of objects faced you and everything else receded to one point. She copied the diagram, generating a street from just a horizon line, one point, and a set of lines fanning out from it, and it looked like a real street for the first time. She made a database of sorts in her notebook, a page of test streets, each one labeled: tall buildings, short buildings, one with trolley tracks.

On Saturday she took her sketchbook to the corner of Miller and Pine to draw from life. She picked the corner because it was interesting, two rows of shops turning away from each other, and she set up her vanishing point in the middle of the page. Then she tried to make the lines meet there. The shopfronts facing her on Miller Street were flat and square, but the row running down Pine angled away at a slant that refused to cooperate. She drew it, erased it, drew it again. Every version came out bent, like the buildings were melting sideways off the page.

She sat on the curb and thought about the gallery painting. In that one, the painter had stood in the middle of the avenue, not at a corner. The fronts of the buildings had faced the viewer square on, and only the side edges had run away to the point. Her corner gave her fronts going in two directions at once, which was interesting but needed something more than one point. That was the difference. She tested it right there: she walked to the middle of Pine Street, stood where she faced straight down it, and sketched fast. The fronts of the shops faced her, the side walls slid back, and every receding line ran to one vanishing point on her page. It worked.

For the contest she drew a street like that, straight on, with a bicycle leaning against a lamppost halfway down. Israel looked at it Monday and said, "That's radical. How'd you figure it out?"

Ruby tapped the small doorway she'd placed at the end of the street. "Everything runs to this," she said. "But only if you stand facing straight down the street. I found that out the hard way at the corner of Pine."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
story:
Leo had wanted the far lab bench by the window, the one where you could see the soccer field, and yesterday he had even shoved Noah's bag off it to claim the spot. Today, standing at the middle bench instead because Ms. Takahashi had reassigned seats, he wondered whether the shove had been worth it. Noah hadn't spoken to him since.

Each bench held a microscope, a razor blade, a tweezers, and half an onion. Ms. Takahashi told them to peel the papery skin from the inside curve, mount it wet on a slide, and stain it with iodine before looking. Then she wrote three words on the board: cell wall, membrane, nucleus.

Leo peeled a strip so thin it was almost invisible, but when he laid it flat the center fold stayed thick and opaque, so he trimmed that part away and kept only the edges. Beside him Noah wrestled with a strip that kept folding on itself. Leo knew he should offer his tweezers, or say something to console him after yesterday, but the words stuck. He bent over the eyepiece instead.

Under the lens the skin broke into a whole parliament of brick-shaped rooms, every wall crisp and neat, rows of them like apartments. Leo's pencil moved, drawing the walls, then the thin line inside each wall for the membrane. Then he stopped. In the middle of every single room sat a small, round, darker spot. He sat back. Was that dirt? He checked the slide for smudges, cleaned the glass with the corner of his shirt, and looked again. The dots were still there, one per room, all round, all small.

"Dirt wouldn't sit in the same spot in every cell," Leo said, half to himself. Noah leaned over and squinted into the lens. "There's one in mine too. In all of them. Maybe it's part of the cell. Like a little control room."

Leo slid the tweezers across the bench without a word. Noah took them, and for a second it felt like the shove had never happened. They flipped through Ms. Takahashi's diagram sheet together and found the label. "That's the nucleus," Noah read. "It holds the cell's genetic material, DNA." Leo copied the word onto his drawing, arrow pointing at the dark dot, then checked the real slide once more against the page. Every room had its dot. He had almost called a real part of the cell dirt.

"Want to swap slides and see if mine shows up better?" Noah asked, holding out his.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
Mya had been saving her question for the school festival all week, because the new kid, Etienne, would be at the international booth, and she wanted to ask him the same thing everyone else did: "Where are you from?" Nobody had gotten a straight answer yet. He'd say "sort of everywhere" and then change the subject.

The festival filled the gym with folding tables, each one a country. Mahi was running the India booth with her grandmother's saris draped over the front. Ms. Jung had set up the Korea booth next to the bake sale. Mya carried her own contribution, a database she'd made for her computer project: a spreadsheet listing every classmate, their family's country, and their favorite food. She thought it was clever until Etienne walked in and she couldn't figure out where to put him.

Etienne had lived in four countries. He'd told the class that on his first day, along with a list of the languages he spoke, but when Mya asked where he was from, he only shrugged. "My parents are from one place, I was born in a different place, and I grew up in two more," he said. "Everyone wants one answer. I don't have one."

Mya sat down next to him at the France booth, which he was supposed to be helping with even though he'd only lived there for two years. She opened her laptop. "Okay, then. I'll make a new column. Instead of one country, I'll write all four, and the years you lived in each." She started typing. "You can't quantify this the way I did with everyone else, one row, one answer."

"It's not a math problem," Etienne said, but he leaned over to watch.

Ms. Jung came by with a plate of food from the Korea booth and stopped when she saw the screen. She asked what they were doing, and Mya explained the database project and the problem of Etienne. "Ah," Ms. Jung said. "There's actually a name for that. Ruth Hill Useem, an American sociologist, coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s." She handed them the plate and went back to her booth.

"A third culture kid," Mya repeated. "For children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. That's you." Etienne read the words off the screen twice. Then he picked up a marker and changed the sign on the France booth, crossing out "France" and writing "Third Culture Kids, booth currently located in France." Mahi came over to see, and two other kids who had wandered between booths all morning gathered too, saying the sign was about them as well. Etienne pulled a chair up to the table and pointed at the empty seat beside him.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
story:
Natalie had written nine drafts of her story about a haunted toothbrush, and she still could not figure out where it went wrong. The writing club met in Ms. Greco's classroom after school on Tuesdays, and today the desks had been pushed into a lopsided circle. Kaden sat across from her, eating crackers he had smuggled in a pencil case, which was against every rule of snack hygiene ever invented.

"Read it out loud," said Emerson, who had brought three highlighters and no actual draft.

Natalie read. The story was about a girl whose toothbrush started whispering at night, warning her that her little brother was secretly a robot. Everyone leaned in at the whispering part. Then the girl brushed her teeth, went to a school dance, argued with a friend about glitter, came home, and trapped the brother in a laundry basket. The end.

"That was radical," said Kaden, crumbs flying. "But weird. It's like the story fell asleep in the middle and then woke up screaming."

Emerson pointed a green highlighter at page two. "The dance scene. That's the climax. It's the longest part, and there's a whole fight about glitter."

"No way," said Kaden. "The laundry basket. Robots in a basket. Obviously the climax is the basket."

They argued for three minutes while Natalie stared at her pages. Then she held up a hand. "Wait. Ms. Greco said one thing about climaxes last week. She said the climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other." She laid the pages side by side on the desk. "So the question isn't which scene is longest or loudest. It's which scene decides things. One way or the other."

Emerson frowned. "But my story last week was super long in the middle and Ms. Greco said the middle was fine."

"That's not the point," said Natalie. She tapped the dance scene. "If I cut this, does anything change? The girl still comes home. The brother is still a robot. Nothing is decided here." Then she tapped the laundry basket scene. "But if I cut this, the brother-robot problem never gets solved. The whole conflict gets decided right here. Basket. That's the climax."

Kaden pumped both fists. "The basket! I said the basket!"

"You said it for the wrong reason," said Emerson, but she was grinning as she said it, and she uncapped the red highlighter and marked the basket scene herself. "Okay. I change my vote."

"So the middle isn't bad," Natalie said slowly, seeing it now. "It's just in the wrong place. The story builds to a whisper, then takes a nap at a glitter dance, then explodes." She pulled out a pen. "What if the dance comes first, as ordinary life, and the whispering starts right after? Then everything climbs toward the basket."

"Or," said Kaden, "the toothbrush whispers during the dance. In front of everyone. Mouth full of toothpaste."

Natalie laughed so hard she knocked over the crackers. "That's disgusting. That's perfect." She started writing before the crumbs even hit the floor, and Ms. Greco leaned over her shoulder, read two lines, and quietly slid the rest of the crackers into her desk drawer.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
Penelope stood at the edge of her aunt's backyard with her phone hidden in her sleeve, mouthing words under the sound of the dhol drum. In three weeks she would stand before the Panj Pyare at her Amrit Sanchar, the Khalsa initiation ceremony, and she was determined to recite Japji Sahib perfectly, all of it, from memory.

"You're perspiring," said her cousin, fanning her with a paper plate. "It's not that hot."

"It's not the heat. It's line forty." Penelope whispered the troublesome words again, then lost them again, like water slipping through her fingers. She had tried reading the prayer fifty times, but somehow her brain only held what she heard.

Then she noticed something. Her grandfather, a veteran of every family wedding and funeral for sixty years, sat by the mango tree reciting along with the aunties, eyes closed, never missing a word. He wasn't reading. He had never once, in her whole life, seen him hold a gutka at a gathering like this. He knew Japji Sahib the way he knew how to breathe.

Her idea arrived like a firecracker. If she stopped reading and only listened, over and over, maybe the words would stick the way they stuck for him.

"Play the recording," she told her cousin, and instead of staring at her phone screen, she closed her eyes through the whole recitation. When the aunties started the verses again for the elders who had arrived late, she kept her eyes shut and let the rhythm pour in. Musk from the incense drifted past. Her sandals stuck slightly to the grass. And then, on the third repetition, her own lips were moving half a second ahead of the sound, the hidden pattern suddenly clear, every verse locking onto the one before it like puzzle pieces she had been holding upside down.

"You got it," her cousin whispered, poking her arm. "You actually got it!"

Payton and Lucas appeared at the fence gate, waving. "We biked over," Payton panted. "Did you finish learning your prayer?"

"Line forty and everything," Penelope said, grinning so wide her cheeks ached. "And I found out something. My mom said the same prayer is recited at the initiation itself. So when I stand there, I won't just be saying something I practiced alone. I'll be saying what everyone says, all together."

Lucas leaned his bike against the fence. "So it's like a secret code you already know."

"More like a song the whole family knows," Penelope said, and she took a deep breath and began, right there in the backyard, the first verse rolling out steady and sure.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: In Excel, a 'bar chart' has horizontal bars and a 'column chart' has vertical bars, although both compare amounts across categories.
story:
On Saturday morning Arianna sat at her mother's desk in the corner of the office, because the library was closed and the rec-center spreadsheet project was due Monday. Marvin had come along, mostly for the vending machine on the third floor, but he pulled a chair up beside her and watched the screen. The center wanted to know which Saturday classes had the most sign-ups so they could order supplies, and Coach had asked for numbers, not guesses.

Arianna typed the class names into column A and the sign-up counts into column B, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the numbers. She remembered the formula from the handout and typed =SUM(B2:B9). The cell showed 186, which matched the total she'd added by hand on paper, so the adding part was done. Now the chart. She highlighted the names and numbers, clicked Insert, and chose the chart that said Bar.

The chart appeared, and the bars ran sideways. Coding stretched across the page, Pottery hung below it, Fencing below that, each one reaching out to the right like arms. "It's lying down," Marvin said. "The whole thing's sideways. Did you break it?"

"No, it's not broken." Arianna leaned closer. The names sat on the left side of the chart, one per row, and every bar grew out to the right from its name. She scrolled through the chart menu again and found a second button, the one that said Column. She was hesitant to click it, since she'd already made a chart and didn't want to lose it, but there was an Undo button if it went wrong. She clicked.

The new chart stood the bars upright. The same names now ran along the bottom, and the bars grew upward, Fencing tallest, then Coding, with Pottery and the rest in a row beside them. "Oh," she said. "They're different. That one's a bar chart, so the bars go across. This one's a column chart, so they stand up." Marvin looked from one version to the other. "Same numbers," he said. "Same amount of tall either way."

Ms. Banerjee, who worked at the desk across the aisle, rolled her chair over and introduced herself as a neighbor who didn't have a home office. She asked to see the chart, said the standing bars would read better in the email to the rec-center board, and added that the numbers needed one small amendment, since the Chess Club count had gone up by four after Thursday. Arianna changed the 12 to a 16, and the total cell jumped to 190 and the Chess bar stretched taller, all by itself. Marvin pointed at the screen. "It fixed its own chart. Now that's going to propel me straight to the vending machine, because I earned it."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Lea sat with her ankle propped on the chair across from her, because she had twisted it jumping off the bleachers during lunch. The jump itself had seemed like a fine idea at the time. Her friend Giuseppe had said, "Don't," and she had said, "Watch me," and now here she was, waiting for Mr. Sánchez to look at a ankle she could have predicted would go sideways.

Her mother had gone to the front desk to sort out the insurance card, so Lea was alone with a rack of pamphlets. She picked one up mostly because the cover showed a brain drawn in blue crayon colors. YOUR DEVELOPING BRAIN, it said. She flipped past the parts she already knew from health class and stopped on a page about the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses. It keeps developing through the teenage years, the pamphlet said, and into a person's twenties.

Lea read the sentence twice. She looked at her ankle, swelling inside her sneaker, and thought about the bleachers. She thought about the boots. Two weeks ago she had taken sixty-three dollars out of the shoebox in her closet, money she had been saving since September for the class trip to the river caves, and spent all of it on silver boots she had seen through a shop window for exactly four minutes before buying them. The boots now sat under her bed, and she was vain enough, she had to admit, to keep wearing them even though Anabelle had pointed out they matched nothing Lea owned. Planning. Controlling impulses. Apparently the part of her that was supposed to handle those jobs was still under construction.

She pulled out her phone and typed a message to Anabelle: "At doctor for ankle. Bleacher thing. Also I read something. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into your twenties. So basically I have construction equipment where decisions should be. Does this mean I can charge the boots to my brain?"

The reply came in three bubbles. "That is the most convenient excuse I have ever heard." Then: "But also, my cousin is 24 and he still eats cereal out of a mixing bowl, so maybe it's true." Then: "Are you still coming to the caves? Because the deposit is due Friday."

Lea looked at the deposit line. Fifty dollars, nonrefundable. The boots had cost sixty-three. She could return them, she realized; the receipt was still in the box, and the store took returns within thirty days. Thirteen dollars would not cover fifty, but babysitting Saturday could contribute the rest if she started now.

The door opened and Mr. Sánchez came out in his white coat. "Lea? Left ankle, I hear. What happened?" His eyes went to the pamphlet still in her hand. "Doing some light reading?"

"Bleachers," she said. "I jumped off them even though my friend said not to." She held up the pamphlet. "Turns out my planning department is a work in progress."

Mr. Sánchez laughed and waved her toward the hallway. "Then we'd better get that ankle sorted so you can plan on walking to the shoe store," he said. "Sounds like you've got boots to return."

Lea limped after him, already typing Anabelle back: "Boots going back tomorrow. Caves are on."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
Lauren stood at the dessert table at her cousin's graduation party, next to a tray of lemon bars her grandmother had made from a recipe on the back of a flour corporation's box. Her uncle Ray took one, bit into it, and made a face.

"Too sour," he announced to the whole backyard. "Nobody likes these."

Lauren looked down the table. Aunt Priya had taken two. Two of the little cousins were eating theirs down to the crumbs. She thought about the science unit Ms. Nowak had assigned before summer break, the one where the class had surveyed 200 students about cafeteria snacks. Lauren had surveyed only her three friends first, and all of them had said they loved the veggie chips, so she'd written that everyone did. Then the big survey came back with different numbers, and Jasmine had laughed so hard she knocked over Ariya's glue. Ms. Nowak hadn't lectured. She'd just handed back both charts side by side and let Lauren look.

She exhaled slowly and counted the plate of lemon bars. Twelve pieces had been set out. Seven were gone, and the party had been going for an hour. Two whole bars sat untouched on her uncle's napkin beside his soda, abandoned after one bite.

"Uncle Ray," she said, "how many people did you actually ask?"

He shrugged. "I asked your dad. He made the same face."

"So that's two people out of, what, forty here?" She pointed at the tray. "Seven bars gone in an hour. And Aunt Priya took seconds."

"The kid did a whole survey," Aunt Priya said from behind them, waving her half-eaten bar. "Look at her, counting everything."

"I'm not doing a survey," Lauren said, though her notebook was already out of her back pocket, the same one she'd carried all spring. She flipped past the snack chart to a clean page and wrote the tally: eaten, refused, unknown. Her uncle watched her with his arms crossed, but he didn't walk away.

"There's melted ice cream on your collar," he said at last, pointing at a molten streak of vanilla running down toward her sleeve.

Lauren blotted it with a napkin and kept counting. Two more people came up for bars while she stood there, one of them the graduate herself, who took a piece in each hand. "Grandma only makes these once a year," the graduate said. "You trying to figure out if she should make them more?"

"Sort of," Lauren said. "I'm trying to figure out what's actually true."

Her uncle picked up his second abandoned bar, turned it over, and took another bite.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
The bus to Camp Wenaki left at seven in the morning, and Hudson had until sundown to prove to himself that he could handle two weeks away. That was why he was at the canoe launch with Ronan and Addisyn, dragging the old aluminum canoe down to the water while the sky turned orange over the far shore. The canoe belonged to the landlord of the marina, who rented it out for five dollars, and Hudson had paid with quarters he had been saving since spring.

"The thing I'm worried about isn't the food or the bugs," Hudson said, steadying the bow. "It's getting lost. My mom says the camp is huge, with a lake and trails everywhere. What if I'm out somewhere at night and I can't tell which way is back?"

Ronan shrugged. "They'd give you a map. Or a counselor."

Addisyn tipped her chin toward the water. "My brother went last year. He said no phones allowed, not even at night. They do this thing where everyone lies on the dock and finds north with just the stars."

"Find north?" Hudson let the canoe drift against the gravel. "How? The stars are everywhere."

"Wouldn't know," Addisyn said. "He wouldn't tell me. He said it would embarrass him to admit he remembered anything from camp."

They paddled out and back, then hauled the canoe up and stayed as the light drained out of the sky. The three of them lay on the wooden planking of the launch, shoulders touching, and Hudson scanned for anything familiar. The Big Dipper came out first, its seven stars bright and easy, hanging above the tree line like a giant ladle.

"There," he said. "But that doesn't tell me anything. It just sits there."

He stared harder. Four stars made the bowl, and he traced them with his finger, one edge, then the other. One side of the bowl ran parallel to the other side, neat and straight. Then he tried something. He lined up his arm with the two stars at the outer edge of the bowl, the ones on the far lip, and slid his hand outward, away from the handle. His arm crossed a stretch of dark sky and stopped at one lone star, brighter than the scattered ones around it, sitting almost exactly where his hand pointed.

"That star," Addisyn said, sitting up. "My brother drew it on a napkin once. He called it Polaris, the North Star."

"It works," Hudson said, half whispering. "The two stars at the edge of the bowl. They point right at it. Every time I trace it, I land on the same star." He did it again to be sure, and again, and his arm stopped in the same place, steady over the trees.

"Great," Ronan said. "Now point south."

Hudson turned his back to Polaris and jabbed a finger toward the dark water below the launch. "That way. And in two weeks I'll be doing this on a dock in the middle of nowhere."

Addisyn flopped back down beside him. "Then find it one more time, so you don't forget."

Hudson raised his arm to the bowl and traced the line, slow and careful, out to the lone steady light.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, most often because the eyeball is slightly too long.
story:
Nathaniel sat on the kitchen counter swinging his legs while his mom peeled the sticker off the new glasses case. The problem had started two weeks ago, in the back row of Ms. Karimi's class, where the board had turned into a soft gray smear. He could read his phone perfectly, which had briefly made him suspect the board itself, maybe dry-erase markers of terrible quality, maybe a chalk conspiracy. Then he'd borrowed Elia's notes and realized the smear followed him everywhere that was far away.

"It's called nearsighted," Marielle had told him at lunch, matter-of-fact, because she'd had glasses since fourth grade. "Light from far stuff focuses in front of your retina instead of on it." She'd tapped her own lenses. "Usually because your eyeball is a tiny bit too long."

"Your eyeball is too long," Nathaniel had replied, and they'd laughed until milk came out of Elia's nose.

Now the glasses were here, and Nathaniel had a theory to test before he even put them on. If the problem was distance, then things up close should look the same either way. He held up his phone with one hand, glasses in the other. Text, sharp. He slid the glasses on. Text, still sharp, maybe smaller. Then he looked out the window at the mailbox across the street, which for weeks had been a friendly blue blob. The mailbox had a flag. The flag was up. "Whoa," he said. "The mail came."

His mom raised an eyebrow. "You thought the mailman was a raccoon?"

"I had no data on the mailman."

He got systematic about it. He walked to the end of the driveway and back, testing the street sign, the neighbors' porch numbers, a squirrel on the fence that turned out to be two squirrels. He made a mental chart. Far things: fixed. Near things: unchanged. Which implied, he decided, that Marielle was right and his eyeballs were, in fact, slightly too long. He went inside and told his mom this with great dignity.

"Congratulations," she said. "Also, since you can see the mailbox now, you're in charge of the mail, which means you'll be the first to see the checks. Our household revenue depends on your new glasses."

"The revenue of this entire house rides on my eyeballs being too long?" He adjusted the glasses, striking what he hoped was a heroic pose. "Then I accept the burden."

He trotted back down the driveway, flags and squirrels and porch numbers all crisp around him, and pulled the mail from the box with a flourish. "Two checks and a pizza menu!" he announced to the whole street.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
story:
Jared's basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and his laptop sat propped on a milk crate between two sleeping bags. "Okay," he said, tapping the keyboard. "Ms. Becker said our project has to run by Friday. Yours asks for a number and says if it's prime. Mine has to do factorials, which is way worse." Jasmine pulled her chair closer, practically bouncing. She had been thinking about prime numbers all day, and tonight she was finally going to make the computer decide them for her.

She typed fast, reading each line out loud as it appeared. "n equals int, input, give me a number. Then for i in range of 2 and n, if n percent i equals zero, print not prime." It felt like casting a spell. "Then print prime at the end," she finished, and hit run before Jared could even grab another handful of popcorn.

The screen asked for a number. Jasmine typed 7, her all-time favorite. "Not prime," the screen announced. She stared at it. "Seven is absolutely prime. Try five." Jared typed 5. Not prime. He typed 11, then 13, then, just to be ridiculous, 2. Not prime, not prime, not prime. "Every single number," Jasmine said. "It thinks nothing is prime. Nothing in the whole world."

Jared flopped backward onto a sleeping bag and groaned at the ceiling, but Jasmine's instinct told her the bug was small and sneaky, hiding somewhere she couldn't see it. She traced the loop with her finger on the screen, her attention suddenly acute. "Wait," she said slowly. "When I type 7, the loop checks i. And range of 2 and 7 goes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. It stops right before 7 itself." She counted on her fingers to be sure. "So it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself." Jared sat up so fast the milk crate wobbled. "Then where does it get the idea that 7 divides by something?"

They stared at the code together, and then Jasmine saw it: her final line, the "print prime" one, was sitting inside the loop by mistake, so the program printed "prime" over and over and then "not prime" last, and the last word was all they'd been reading. "It was saying prime the whole time," she shouted, laughing. "We just watched the wrong part!" She yanked the last print statement out of the loop, aligned it with the "for" line, and ran it again. Seven went in. Prime, said the screen, once, clean and certain. Jared held up the popcorn bowl like a trophy, and Jasmine reached over and typed 97, just because she couldn't wait to see it one more time.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Rachel had been staying at Grandma's house for three days, and she had one clear objective: learn to do an entire load of laundry by herself before her mother arrived on Saturday. Grandma had shown her the sorting part on Monday, dark clothes in one pile and light clothes in another, and Rachel had felt optimistic about the whole project until she opened the bleach bottle that afternoon.

The striped shirt was the problem. It was Ahmed's, borrowed for a paint fight at Jericho's birthday party, and now it was streaked with grey smudges. Rachel figured bleach would brighten it right up, but when she flipped the shirt over, she found a care label with a triangle crossed out with a big X. She stared at it. On her own white socks, the label showed a plain empty triangle, no X at all. So the symbols were opposites. The crossed one had to mean no bleach, and the empty one had to mean bleach was fine. She set Ahmed's shirt on the far side of the counter, away from the bottle, feeling like she had cracked a secret code.

Then she found the note on the fridge, held up by the magnet shaped like a trout. "Gone to the garden centre," Grandma had written in her looping hand. "Monitor the washer, it makes a clicking sound on the spin cycle but it's harmless. Your friend's shirt is on the counter, don't bleach it, the label says not to." Rachel laughed out loud. Grandma had known about the shirt the whole time.

But when Rachel went back to the counter, the striped shirt was gone. She checked the hamper, the sofa, even the freezer, because Grandma sometimes put things in strange places. Nothing. Then she heard the clicking sound from the laundry room, a steady tick like a clock with a limp, and noticed the washer's round window full of swirling water. Floating inside, unmistakably, were Ahmed's stripes. Rachel pressed her forehead to the cool glass. Grandma, in her hurry, must have tossed it in with the whites and, worse, Rachel could smell the sharp bleach smell already in the room.

She yanked the dial to drain and pulled the shirt out, dripping and smelling like a swimming pool. The stripes were still stripes, thank goodness, but faintly faded at the collar. Rachel laid it across the porch railing in the sun to dry, and when Grandma's car rattled up the driveway, Rachel was standing beside it, holding the bottle of bleach like evidence.

"I read the label before you did," Rachel said. "The crossed-out triangle means don't bleach."

Grandna picked up the shirt, turned it over, and squinted at the label. "Well," she said slowly, "then we'd best write Ahmed an apology and ask him what he wants for dinner when he comes Friday."

Rachel went inside to find a pen.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: An "upstander" is someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated, instead of only watching as a bystander.
story:
Grandpa's tropical fish tank hummed in the corner while Emmett stared at his phone, reading Otto's messages for the third time. At lunch today, some kids had mimicked the way Kaliyah talked with her hands, and Emmett had just sat there, frozen, until the bell rang. Otto had laughed along, which somehow felt worse.

"You're wearing a hole in that couch," Grandpa said from his armchair.

"Kaliyah got teased today. I didn't do anything." Emmett turned the phone over. "Otto laughed. I didn't even say stop."

Grandpa set down his newspaper. "Tomorrow's another lunch."

That night Emmett lay awake testing an idea, the way he tested things in science class. If he yelled at the teasers, they'd just switch targets, probably to him, and then there'd be two people getting laughed at. If he did nothing again, Kaliyah would keep eating alone. There had to be a move in between. He thought about the fish tank, how the little striped fish always swam near the slow one, not fighting the bigger fish, just staying close so it wasn't alone.

At lunch the next day, he got his chance. The same kids started up again, copying Kaliyah's hand movements. Emmett walked over and sat down directly across from her.

"Kaliyah, did you finish the science questions?" he asked, loud enough to carry. "I got stuck on number four."

The mimicking stuttered and stopped. Kaliyah blinked, then flipped open her notebook. "Number four? That one took me forever. I'll show you." One of the teasers tried another wave of his hands, but with Emmett there asking real questions, nobody laughed, and enforcing the joke suddenly took too much effort. The kid shrugged and turned back to his own table.

Otto lingered, looking unsure.

"Sit or don't," Emmett said. "But knock it off either way."

Otto sat. He even asked Kaliyah about the science homework, and by the end of lunch his ears were red with embarrassment, though he kept talking anyway.

In Ms. Ong's class that afternoon, they discussed a news story about a student who had filmed a bullying incident instead of helping. "Someone who only watches is a bystander," Ms. Ong said, "but someone who speaks up or acts to support a person being mistreated is called an upstander."

Emmett raised his hand. "So an upstander doesn't have to fight anybody? They can just, like, sit with the person?"

"That counts," Ms. Ong said.

After class, Otto caught up with him in the hall. "So at lunch, when you sat with her. Was that being an upstander?"

"That was the whole idea," Emmett said, and shoved open the door to the bus loop, where Kaliyah was waiting with her notebook, already flipped to number four.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
