Nora had never been to her grandmother's town before, and she arrived in Japan in the middle of August, which felt like the worst possible timing. Back home, her teacher Ms. Ramos had told the class about a festival honoring ancestors, and Chanelle had looked it up later and said it happened in July. Nora had stared at her phone for a whole minute, thinking she had missed her one chance. "I thought I'd be too late," she told Ayden on a video call the night before they left Tokyo. "If it's in July, then Grandma already came and went, and I wasn't even here."

Ayden leaned closer to his screen. "So ask somebody there. Maybe it's like time zones."

"That's not a real thing," Nora said, but the idea propelled her downstairs anyway, where her aunt was folding yukata cloths into a bag.

Her aunt laughed a little, the way people do when a worry turns out to be smaller than it sounded. "In some regions it's July," she said. "Here, and in most of Japan, we do Obon in mid-August. Your grandmother's spirit is believed to come home for a visit. You haven't missed anything." Nora let out a breath she felt like she'd been holding since the funeral, three months and one ocean ago.

The temple grounds were crowded by the time they arrived, lanterns strung between wooden posts, drummers tuning their rhythm behind a raised platform. Nora held the paper lantern her aunt had bought and turned it over in her hands, checking for instructions. A woman at the long table, notorious in the family for never letting anyone skip a step, showed Nora how to write her grandmother's name with the brush. Chanelle had texted that morning: "Light it good, ambassador of our whole friend group." Nora had rolled her eyes, but now, carefully painting each character, she sat up straighter, as if her whole class might somehow see her.

She had a theory, and she tested it quietly while she worked. If spirits come home for a visit, she thought, then they must need a path, and that must be what the lanterns were for, a trail of light from the temple back to the house where Grandma lived. So after lighting hers, Nora watched which way the older families carried theirs, and she walked the same direction, holding her lantern up, letting its small flame bob beside her aunt's.

At her grandmother's house, her aunt set her own lantern by the gate. Nora put hers next to it, then looked up at the dark windows. "She'll know it's mine," Nora said. "I used the good brush." Her aunt bumped her shoulder gently, and together they stood in the lantern light, listening to the drums drift down from the temple.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Isaac had claimed the big table by the library window, the one with an outlet, because his science fair project required a lamp, two trays of bean sprouts, and a certain amount of dignity. His hypothesis, printed neatly on an index card, said that the sprouts under the lamp would grow taller than the sprouts in the dark corner by the biographies. It was an influential hypothesis, at least among the four people who had heard it. Marco had declared it "basically guaranteed," which Isaac now understood was not a warranty of any kind.

The problem was the ruler. The dark-corner sprouts were winning. Not by a little, either. The tallest one had gone pale and weird and stretched almost nine centimeters, while the lamp sprouts sat there being green and short and smug about it. Isaac measured them twice, hoping he had measured wrong, and then a third time, which was the scientific version of asking the question again until you liked the answer.

"I could just switch the trays," Marco said, leaning over the table. "Nobody would know."

"The ruler would know," Isaac said. He did not actually believe the ruler had opinions, but at this point he wasn't ruling anything out.

He was carrying the trays toward Ms. Rahman's desk, possibly to confess, possibly to ask if the library had a book called What To Do When Nature Embarrasses You, when she looked up from a return cart and said, before he even spoke, "Let me guess. Wrong direction?" She examined his index card, then his trays, and shrugged. "A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting." Then she went back to scanning books, as if she hadn't just handed him the only useful sentence of his entire week.

Isaac sat down and thought about that while Marco tried to dismiss it. "So you're going to stand up there and tell everyone you were wrong?" Marco said. "In front of the judges?"

"The judges are scientists," Isaac said. "Half their papers are probably titled Well, That Didn't Work." He crossed out nothing on the index card. Instead he wrote a new line under the hypothesis, in careful print: RESULT: OPPOSITE. TALLER IN DARK. He taped the pale nine-centimeter sprout's photo next to it, because the thing had earned its portrait.

At the fair, the judges stopped at his table longer than at anyone else's. One of them leaned in, read the crossed-out prediction and the honest result, and asked Isaac what he would test next. Isaac slid a fresh index card across the table. It said: WHY DO THEY STRETCH? He tapped it twice.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Most bicycle tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air, so a flat usually means a hole in the tube.
story:
Sarah stood in her grandfather's driveway with the front wheel of her bike in her hands and exactly three hours before the trail ride with Josiah and Nikolai. The tyre was as flat as a dropped pancake. She had assumed she would need a whole new tyre, which the bike shop in town might not even have, and the shop closed at one.

"You could dismantle it and look inside," her grandfather said from the porch, and then he went back to his newspaper, because he believed people learned better when nobody hovered. Sarah found a plastic tub under his workbench labelled TYRE STUFF, and inside it were three flat plastic levers, a hand pump, a tin of patches, and a folded note in her grandfather's handwriting.

"Turn the wheel and look for what punctured the tyre," the note said. "If you find glass or a thorn, leave it in that spot. Then take the tyre off and find the hole. Most tyres have a separate inner tube inside that holds the air, so the flat is usually a hole in the tube, not the tyre. Patch the tube. Grandad."

Sarah read the note twice. So there was a tube hiding in there, and that was probably all that was broken. She pushed one lever under the edge of the tyre, then a second, and the tyre loosened enough for her to peel it back. A rubber tube sat inside, grey and sad and soft. She pulled it out and felt along it with her fingers while the clock in the kitchen ticked toward noon. Nothing. She was about to pump air into it and listen for a hiss when she remembered the note's advice about looking for the cause. She spun the wheel slowly, and there, wedged in the tread, was a tiny sliver of glass, thin as a fingernail clipping. It was almost invisible until the sun caught it.

"Got you," she said out loud. She marked the spot with her thumb, pulled the glass out with tweezers, and matched that point on the tyre to the same stretch of tube. When she dipped that section into a bowl of water and squeezed, a thin chain of bubbles rose up, showing the hole like a secret being told.

She roughed the spot with sandpaper, stuck on a patch, and pressed until her thumbs ached. It seemed hopeless pressing a sticker onto rubber and expecting it to hold air, but her grandfather had once told an anecdote about crossing the whole county on a patched tube, so she kept at it. She worked the tube back inside the tyre, tucked the edge under with the levers, and pumped until the tyre was firm. When she squeezed it, it held, round and stubborn.

Josiah rang the doorbell at half past one, two and a half hours early, with his own bike and Nikolai's in tow. "We thought you'd be walking to the trail," he admitted. Sarah carried the wheel out, dropped it into the forks, and spun it. It hummed.

"Tube's patched," she said. "Let's go."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet.
story:
The cardboard carrier wobbled in Theodore's hands as he crossed the backyard, and something inside it yawned so loudly that Kimberly laughed from the porch steps. The kitten was a scrawny gray thing the shelter had named Pocket, and Theodore had spent his savings on her because nobody else wanted a cat with a notched ear. There was only one problem, and it sat in the middle of the kitchen table like a stone: his whole family was vegetarian, and his mom had already said the kitten could just eat what they ate. Lentils, rice, vegetables.

"It's a dilemma," Theodore admitted to Kimberly and Elisha, who had come over to see the new arrival. He let Pocket out onto the grass, where she stalked a falling maple seed with terrifying seriousness. "Everybody at home thinks it's fine, but she's not everybody. She's a cat." He had a vague feeling about it, nothing he could point to, just the memory of Pocket ignoring the shelter worker's offering of bread crust while demolishing a bowl of meat food in ninety seconds flat.

Elisha crouched down and offered Pocket a piece of carrot. Pocket sniffed it, sneezed, and walked away with her tail up like a flag of contempt. "Okay," Elisha said. "That's data."

Theodore had brought out the small bag of food the shelter had sent home, and he read the label aloud on his knees in the grass. "Cats are obligate carnivores," he read. Kimberly frowned, so he said it again, slower. "Obligate carnivores." Whatever it meant, the word obligate sounded like something you couldn't argue with, like a law. The label went on in smaller print, and it said plainly that cats depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet. He read that part twice, feeling the sentence settle over him. It wasn't an opinion. It was the same for every cat that had ever lived.

"So I have to allocate part of my allowance to real cat food," Theodore said. "Every week. Meat food, even though we don't eat it." He did the math in his head, then out loud for Kimberly to check, and she nodded. It would cost most of what he earned walking Ms. Zhang's dog, but he could do it.

That evening he set two bowls on the back step: one with leftover rice and beans, one with the shelter food. Pocket circled both, sniffed the beans, and then drove her whole face into the meat bowl, purring so hard her notched ear trembled. From the kitchen window his mom watched, arms crossed, and finally called through the screen, "Add it to the shopping list. The good kind."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
Mr. Campbell-Brown had written two words on the board in capital letters: FORESHADOWING and SYMBOLISM. "Your essay is mandatory," he said, "and no, you cannot write 'the paw is spooky' three hundred times and call it done." Wyatt slumped. Reading had never intimidated him before, but explaining hidden stuff on paper felt like being asked to describe a smell over the phone.

At lunch, Miriam and Manha spread the photocopies across the cafeteria table. "Okay," Manha said, tapping the page, "our story is The Monkey's Paw, by W. W. Jacobs, from 1902. This soldier guy, Sergeant-Major Morris, shows up at the family's house with this dried old monkey's paw."

"And he literally warns them," Miriam said, reading out loud, "'the wishes bring terrible results.' Then he chucks it into the fire." She flipped the page. "And the dad goes and fishes it out anyway. Like grabbing a hot coal because you like the color."

Wyatt stared at the fire scene for a long moment. "Wait," he said slowly. "That's the foreshadowing, isn't it? Morris didn't just tell them the wishes were bad. He warned them and threw the paw into the fire before they even made one wish. So when everything goes wrong later, you can't say nobody saw it coming. The story told us everything up front."

Manha grinned. "And the fire bit is symbolism too. Getting thrown into the fire is like the paw getting rejected, and the dad rescuing it is like him ignoring the warning." She paused. "That sounded smarter in my head."

"It sounded smart out loud too," Miriam said. "Write that down before one of us forgets it."

Wyatt scribbled notes so fast his pen tore the paper a little. Then he stopped. "Here's my test. If the foreshadowing works, then the dad should have known better. He rescued the paw with his own hand after a soldier who'd actually seen the results told him it was terrible. So every bad thing after that is on him." He looked up. "Is that an argument or am I just being mean to a fictional dad?"

"That's an argument," Miriam said. "A brutal one, but an argument."

On Monday, Mr. Campbell-Brown handed the essays back. Wyatt got an A minus, with one comment in red ink: "Strong reasoning. One deduction for calling Mr. White 'a Paw Goblin of poor choices.'" Wyatt held it up for the others to see, and Manha laughed so hard she knocked over the class plant.

"Symbolism," Wyatt said solemnly, rescuing the pot from the floor. "The fall foreshadowed your detention."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
The message pinged at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, while Jasmine was supposed to be finishing her math homework. It was a screenshot from Mikaella, dropped into the group chat with no caption: a glossy ad for the VivaTab Plus. Five feature bubbles floated across the page. Fastest processor in its class. Superthin design. Award-winning screen. Free streaming bundle. Six-month warranty.

"OK this is the one," Mikaella typed. "I'm asking my parents for it for my birthday."

Jasmine leaned closer to her phone. Something about the ad felt too shiny, the way a lake looks smooth until you poke it with a stick. She typed back, "It does look good. But isn't it weird that there are exactly five great things and nothing else? Like, where's the price of the bad stuff?"

"What bad stuff?" Mikaella replied.

"That's the thing. We don't know. That's what I want to find out."

Marie-Soleil popped into the chat a minute later. "My cousin works at an electronics store. Want me to ask her what people complain about?" Jasmine did want, very much. Mikaella sent a shrug emoji and said, "It has five awards though. Five."

Jasmine chewed on that. Why did the number five keep being mentioned, and why did it make the tablet seem so great? She imagined a corporation somewhere choosing exactly which five facts to put on the page and quietly not choosing the others. It was like the five coolest kids at school saying a party was amazing while nobody mentioned that the music stopped at nine. She typed, "Do you think they listed everything about it, or just the good parts?"

"Obviously just the good parts," Mikaella wrote. "It's an ad."

"But that's the trick," Jasmine typed. "They only show the facts that support their side and leave out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is. There's a name for it. Card stacking."

"Like stacking a deck," Marie-Soleil replied. "So the good cards are always on top."

"Exactly. So let's flip the deck over."

Jasmine opened a review site and searched for VivaTab Plus problems. The first three results made her sit straight up. Owners complained that the battery drained in about four hours. Four! The ad never mentioned battery life at all, not once, and now she understood why. It also ran hot if you watched videos for more than an hour, and the streaming bundle auto-charged your card after three months unless you cancelled. She pasted the links into the chat.

Mikaella was quiet for a long moment. Then: "four hours?? my brother uses his tablet the WHOLE bus ride there and back."

"Plus homework time," Jasmine typed. "The battery would be extinct before dinner."

Marie-Soleil's cousin texted her the same thing: customers came back complaining about the battery more than anything else. "My cousin says the company that makes it probably knows and just doesn't put it in the ads."

"Because they don't have to," Jasmine wrote. She stared at her screen, almost pleased with the feeling of having caught something that had been designed not to be caught. It was a little like finding the hidden picture in one of those magic-eye posters.

The next morning Mikaella came to school with a new plan. "I showed my dad the complaints and the ad side by side, and he said if I can wait for the sale, I can get a different one with a real battery. He says he'll cherish the money I just saved him." She dropped into her seat and pulled out her phone. "Now help me check the ad for the other one. Ten to one they stacked that deck too."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
Katherine exploded off the line like the eight hundred metres was a fifty-metre sprint. For one glorious lap she was in front, her sneakers slapping the gym floor, Gregory's shout ringing behind her. Then the second lap began, and her legs turned to wet sand. She crossed the line in fifth place and had to lean against the bleachers just to stay upright.

Her objective for the next three weeks was simple: figure out what happened in that second lap. She couldn't see the problem, because her legs weren't hurting on purpose and nobody was tripping her, but something invisible was stealing her energy. So she started writing down lap times after every practice run in the gym, hers and Jayda's, on the back of her homework planner.

Jayda always finished stronger than she started. Katherine always faded. One afternoon they compared their splits from the same practice race, and the pattern jumped out at her. "You ran the second lap faster than the first," Katherine said, tapping the numbers. "Every single time. I do the opposite." Jayda grinned and said, "Ms. Moretti calls that a negative split. When you run the first half faster, like you, that's a positive split." Katherine stared at the paper. The names felt backwards, but the times didn't lie.

So she tested a simple idea. In the next practice, she would hold back on the first lap on purpose, keeping Jayda's shoulder a few steps ahead of her, and save everything for the second. It felt wrong at first, like standing still while a race happened somewhere else. When the bell that marked the halfway point rang, she adjusted her stride, pushed her arms harder, and began to hunt.

Gregory, jogging the outside lane as a pacer, yelled, "You've got more than you think!" Her breathing was ragged but her legs still answered. She passed two classmates on the far curve, then a third on the straight. She didn't win, but her second lap was two whole seconds faster than her first, written in her own handwriting in the planner afterward.

At the next time trial, she did it again, and this time she won her heat. Jayda thumped her on the back, and even the coach, who rarely said much, nodded from the doorway. Katherine was starting to believe she had the constitution of a distance runner after all, not because she was the fastest girl in the gym, but because she could wait when waiting was the harder thing.

She stood at the line for the final practice of the unit, planner tucked under her arm, and glanced at Jayda in the next lane. "Watch my second lap," she said, and settled into her crouch.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Chase had six dollars in his pocket and one plan: strawberries for his mom's birthday shortcake. At the first stall in the farmers' market, the baskets were piled high and red, more baskets than he had ever seen in one place. A hand-written sign read three dollars each. He stared at it, because last month, the Saturday he'd forgotten his wallet, the same baskets had been six dollars. He checked the sign twice, as if the number might be shy and change back when noticed.

"Something wrong with them?" he asked the farmer, a woman in a sun hat.

"They're fine. Best ones of the year. I've got more than I know what to do with right now."

Chase walked on to think, past a stall where a tiny wind turbine spun on a pole, powering a fan that kept the greens crisp. The whole market smelled like peaches and kettle corn. He turned the price over in his head. Six dollars last month, three dollars today. It wasn't the strawberries that had changed. They looked better than ever. Something behind the sign had changed, something he couldn't see: how many the farmers had to sell. When there were tons of them, the price dropped. When there were only a few, it climbed. He felt like he'd found a hidden lever under the whole market.

He found his friend Lionel by the honey stall, guarding a jar like it was treasure. "Lionel. Test my theory. Ask the blueberry people what they cost in July."

"July's when blueberries are everywhere," Lionel said. "My grandma freezes bags of them. She calls it stock-up season."

"So in July they're cheap because everybody's got them, and now they're expensive because hardly anybody does." Chase counted on his fingers, adding it up like a cumulative score. "It works for strawberries too. June strawberries, three dollars. They cost double that before, when the stands had just a few."

"You've been doing math on a Saturday," Lionel said. "Voluntarily. I'm telling Mr. Das."

Mr. Das, their neighbor, was two stalls down buying tomatoes, and he raised an eyebrow when the boys told him. "You two figured that out from baskets of fruit? Some people take an economics class to learn it." He held up his tomatoes. "Want to know what these cost me in August?"

"Cheaper," both boys said at once. "Peak harvest."

Chase went back to the strawberry stall and bought two baskets, then a third, because at three dollars he could. The farmer threw in a few bruised ones for free, which would go in the smoothies he'd make to prolong the birthday weekend into Sunday. On the way out, he passed the pie stall, where a line stretched ten people long and the pies were eight dollars each. He nudged Lionel.

"Only so many pies, all those people. You know what that means."

Lionel groaned. "It means we'd better get in line now, before the price finds out."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects; weighing flour is more accurate.
story:
Savannah stood in the baking aisle holding two bags of flour and a small kitchen scale that cost more than her allowance for two weeks. Last Saturday her chocolate chip cookies had come out dry and cakey, more like biscuits than cookies, and her little brother had eaten exactly one and pushed the plate away. She was in charge of dinner and dessert tonight while her parents worked late, and she did not want a repeat.

Mr. Wu from next door turned into the aisle with his cart, and she felt a flash of relief at seeing a familiar face.

"Buying a scale?" he asked, nodding at the box.

"My cookies were wrong," Savannah said. "The recipe said two and a quarter cups, and I measured exactly that. Two and a quarter cups, level with a knife and everything." She caught herself remembering how she had dug the measuring cup straight down into the flour bag, packing it full, and how proud she'd been of the neat flat top. Now that memory provoked an uneasy feeling, like she'd checked the wrong answer twice and called it right.

Mr. Wu smiled. "My grandmother broke me of scooping flour straight from the bag. She weighed everything."

Savannah frowned. Scooping did something? She turned the flour bag over in her hands, thinking. If she pushed the cup down into the bag, the flour would get packed down, and a packed cup could hold more flour than the recipe expected. More flour than the recipe wanted. That would make cookies dry. Dry and cakey. She looked up at Mr. Wu, and he gave her the small nod of a man watching a jury reach a verdict.

"Could I borrow your scale tonight?" she asked. "I'll bring it back tomorrow."

"You can borrow mine and keep the one in your cart," he said. "Two scales, two tests."

At home, she laid both scales on the counter and set out two identical measuring cups. Into the first cup she scooped flour straight from the bag, digging deep and leveling it off. Into the second she spooned flour gently, the way the recipe book's small-print note suggested, and leveled that too. Then she weighed them. The scooped cup was heavier, a lot heavier, close to a whole extra half cup's worth of flour hiding inside what looked like the same measurement. She wrote both numbers on the back of a receipt, because her brother, who was already circling the mixing bowl with his spoon, would never believe her otherwise.

She weighed the flour for the new batch straight into the bowl, no cups at all, checking the number against the recipe. The dough came out softer and shinier, and it smelled like actual cookie dough instead of paste. Her brother hovered nearby, spoon raised, his judgment momentarily vulnerable to the smell of butter and brown sugar.

"Try one," she said, sliding the first warm cookie off the sheet.

He bit into it, chewed, and pointed the spoon at the plate. "Make these forever."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
Every morning that week, Gabriella had found the strawberries in her backyard patch half-eaten, and this morning two whole berries were gone. She crouched over the flattened leaves and called across the fence, "Zackery! Get over here! We have a mystery."

Zackery bolted through the gap in the hedge, still holding his toast. "Raccoons," he said. "Definitely raccoons. That's my theory."

"Your what?" Gabriella squinted at him.

"Theory. Like, a fancy guess." He shrugged. "My brother says scientists don't know anything anyway. He says evolution is just a theory, so it's basically a guess."

Gabriella ran inside, grabbed her science notebook, and came back flipping pages. Earlier that year Ms. Castillo had made them copy a sentence from the board, and Gabriella had underlined it twice. She held it out. "Look. It says a theory is not a guess, it's an explanation that's been tested over and over and supported. A hypothesis is the idea that's still being tested."

"So a hypothesis is the guess part," Zackery said slowly, "and a theory is the part that already passed the tests?"

"Right. So your raccoon thing isn't even a theory. It's a hypothesis. And we can test it." She was already pacing the length of the patch. "If raccoons did this, they'd climb the fence, so we'd find muddy prints on the rails. If it was birds, they'd peck from above and leave the top of the berries torn up. These bites are on the side, low, near the ground."

Zackery checked the fence rails. "No prints. That contradicts raccoons."

They tested it that night. Gabriella's dad adjusted the thermostat on his way out to the porch, muttering that he wasn't sitting in the cold, so the porch light glowed warm and yellow over the garden while they hid behind the shed with a thermos of cocoa. Elliana squeezed in beside them at ten o'clock because she'd heard about the stakeout and refused to miss it. "If it's rabbits," she whispered, "there'll be droppings by morning. My aunt says check for droppings."

At 10:40 the grass rustled. Something small and brown hopped out of the dark, sat up on its hind legs, and plucked a strawberry clean off the plant with its teeth.

"Rabbit!" all three of them hissed at once, and the rabbit froze, then vanished into the hedge with the berry still in its mouth.

Gabriella wrote in her notebook by porch light: Hypothesis, raccoons, overturned. Hypothesis, rabbits, supported. Not a theory yet. Not until we test it again. "Tomorrow night," she said, "we put a low fence around the patch and see if it holds. If the berries survive, that's test number two."

Elliana grinned. "And if a rabbit gets in anyway?"

"Then we make a new hypothesis and start over." Gabriella snapped the notebook shut. "Science isn't one big guess that stays a guess forever. It's guesses you keep checking until they can't be knocked down."

Zackery raised his cocoa. "To test number two," he said. "No permanent conclusions until the rabbits say so."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: In a three-point argument, each point usually gets its own body paragraph, which opens with a topic sentence linking that point back to the thesis.
story:
Rachel sat at the kitchen table with a blank page and a pencil that had already been sharpened twice. Her assignment was to write an argument for why the school should start a compost bin, but Mr. Zhou had refused to let anyone draft a single sentence yet. First they needed a thesis, then three points, then an outline. Rachel had a thesis: "Our school should compost its cafeteria waste." She had scribbled four possible points and crossed out two. What she did not have was any idea how the outline was supposed to hold together.

The doorbell rang, and Charlee came in still holding her lacrosse stick, because she wanted Rachel's dad to drive them both to Saturday's game. He wasn't home yet, so she flopped into the chair across from Rachel and peered at the page. "You have three things written here," Charlee said. "What do they do?"

"They're my points," Rachel said. "Composting cuts trash, teaches science, and gives the garden free fertilizer." She stared at the list. Three points, and then a whole essay to write, and no clue how to connect them. She assumed each point would just turn into sentences somewhere, floating around in the draft until it looked long enough.

A scratchy sound came from the back porch, then silence. Rachel stood very still, listening. The yard looked tranquil in the late light, the compost bucket beside the door with its lid on tight. The sound came again, closer, and Charlee gripped her stick. Something was out there, and neither of them could see it.

Rachel ignored it for one more minute because an idea had just landed in her head, whole and shining. She grabbed a clean sheet and wrote her thesis at the top. Then, under it, she wrote the first point and started a paragraph. The paragraph opened with "First, composting cuts our school's trash in half," which was a sentence that tied the point back to her thesis. She did the same for the second and third points, and suddenly she saw it: each point got its own paragraph, and each paragraph opened with a sentence that linked back to the thesis. "Give me your highlighter," she said, and Charlee dug one from her bag. Rachel marked the first sentence of every paragraph.

"Read only the yellow parts," she said, and held out the page. Charlee read the thesis, then the three highlighted sentences, and her eyebrows went up. "I skipped everything else and I still got your whole argument. It's like a skeleton."

"The first sentences are topic sentences," Rachel said. "I just tested it on you." The scratchy sound came again, and Charlee was already at the window. "Rach," she said. "Your compost bucket lid is moving."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
Luke pressed his nose to the glass case and read the label twice. "Mystery liquids," it said. "Use the litmus paper to test each one." A science museum was not where he had wanted to spend his Saturday, but his mother had dropped him off with Paxton and Maddie anyway, and Mr. Mokoena from next door had promised to pick them up at four. That gave them three hours and one puzzle: twelve bottles, no labels that helped, and a stack of thin paper strips beside a color chart numbered zero to fourteen.

"Red means acid," Maddie said, pointing at the chart. "Blue means base. Middle is neutral." She was reading fast, the way she did before anyone could beat her to an answer. Paxton had already dipped a strip into bottle one, which fizzed faintly. The strip turned pink.

Luke picked up bottle seven, which looked like plain water but smelled faintly of soap. He thought of his grandfather's bathroom sink, where a sliver of white soap sat in a dish and the whole room smelled like that. One evening last week he had run the water over the sliver and dropped in one of the litmus strips from his backpack kit, just to see. The strip had turned blue, deep blue, and the chart in his kit had put it around nine or ten. Vinegar, which he had also tested, turned red and sat way down near the other end. Soapy water and vinegar were on opposite sides of the scale. He hadn't believed it at first, because soap feels gentle and acid sounded like the dangerous one.

"Bet it's neutral," Paxton said, leaning over bottle seven. "Looks like water."

"It won't be," Luke said. "Watch." He dipped the strip, counted to five like the chart instructions said, and held it up. Blue. He laid it against the chart. "Nine, maybe ten. Most regular bar soap is basic, around nine or ten on the pH scale." Paxton squinted at the strip, then at the chart, then back at the strip.

"Okay," Paxton said slowly. "I thought acids were the strong ones. Soap's on the opposite side from vinegar, and it's still up there." He grabbed bottle eight and a fresh strip, suddenly in a hurry to test his own guess about the dish soap inside it. Maddie wrote "7: soap, 9-10" in the little notebook she carried everywhere, then ruled a line for bottle eight and waited, pencil ready.

By the time Mr. Mokoena arrived, they had worked through all twelve bottles. Maddie had filled six notebook pages, Paxton had changed his mind about three guesses, and Luke was explaining that bacteria could colonize the drain in the museum's fountain display, which was why the water smelled strange, though that was a test for another day. Mr. Mokoena asked what an extravagant afternoon of chemistry had cost them, and Luke held up the plastic bag of used strips like a trophy.

"Nothing," he said. "We didn't even break anything."

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups, so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised.
story:
Kate sat on the counter stool at Mr. Rahimi's phone repair shop, her laptop open next to a tray of tiny screws. She had spent two weeks collecting survey answers from students about the school cafeteria, and now she had to turn three hundred rows of responses into something the principal would actually read.

"You said a pivot table would summarize them," she said. "By grade."

Mr. Rahimi wiped his hands on a cloth and came over. "Make a column for grade, a column for the answer, then drop them into the rows and values. It counts for you." He pointed at a cracked phone on his bench. "While you try it, I'm going to simulate a drop test on that one. It's hypothetical until the screen actually cracks."

Kate selected her data, inserted the pivot table, and dragged "Grade" into the rows area and "Favorite cafeteria meal" into the values area. The summary appeared instantly. She scrolled down the short list: Grade 6, Grade 7, Grade 8.

Then she counted again. Grade 6 had 112 responses. Grade 8 had 104. Grade 7 showed only 41, and below it sat a second row, "Gr 7," with 43.

"That's wrong," she said. "Grade seven only shows forty-one, but I collected eighty-four of those."

Mr. Rahimi leaned over without touching the keyboard. "Looks like your table thinks you have six grades."

Kate stared at the two rows. They looked the same to her. Then she went back to her raw data and sorted the grade column. The entries scrolled past: Grade 6, Grade 6, Gr 7, Grade 8, Gr 7, Grade 6. Some students had typed it one way, some the other. She hadn't noticed because on paper the difference was small.

She tested a simple idea. She used find and replace, changing every "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", then refreshed the pivot table. The two rows merged into one that read 84.

"So it wasn't counting wrong," she said. "It was treating them as two different grades because the words weren't typed the same."

"Exactly," Mr. Rahimi said. "The table only knows what the words say, not what you mean by them."

The door chimed and Alanna came in, shaking rain off her jacket. "Did you finish the numbers? Hillary wants to know if pizza actually won."

"Pizza won in grade six and eight," Kate said, turning the screen. "But grade seven picked the noodle bar by ten votes, and I almost missed it. Half their answers were hiding in a separate row."

Alanna frowned at the screen. "Why would it split them?"

"Because 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' count as two different things. I had to make them match first." Kate copied the finished table into her report, then saved the file twice, once to her laptop and once to a drive in her backpack, next to a paperback with a cracked spine she kept meaning to tape.

Mr. Rahimi set the dropped phone back on the bench, its screen intact. "Hypothetical no more," he said.

Kate zipped her bag. "Tomorrow I'm checking every column before I summarize anything. Hillary's survey is next, and she spells 'seventh' three different ways."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
story:
Eleanor's laptop sat on the kitchen table next to a bowl of cereal she had stopped eating an hour ago. On the screen was her Python program, which was supposed to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and which currently believed that 9 was prime.

"You typed equals-equals, right?" Gurshaan said over video call. "Last week Japji spent forty minutes on one equals sign."

"I typed it right," Eleanor said. "It's the loop. Watch." She entered 9 again, and the program printed "prime" with total confidence.

Japji leaned closer on his screen. "It only checks 2, then it stops."

Eleanor read her own code. She had written the loop to test divisors 2, 4, 6, and so on up to the number itself. If the number wasn't divisible by 2, it sailed through the rest of the even divisors untouched and got declared prime, because 9 was never going to be divisible by 4 or 6 or 8 either.

"Wait," she said slowly. "That's why 9 passed. Nine isn't even divisible by any even number at all."

"So make it count by ones," Gurshaan said.

"I could." Eleanor was already typing. "But if it has to check every single number up to a million, it'll take forever. Ms. Li said ours would be the fanciest prime checker in the grade, and I intend to acquire that title." She paused. "After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one."

There was a silence while Gurshaan and Japji considered this.

"So you check 2 once," Japji said, "then 3, 5, 7, and skip everything even?"

"Half the work, gone." Eleanor changed her loop. "My premise is that 9 gets caught by 3." She ran it.

9: not prime.

She tried 7. Prime. She tried 25, which got caught by 5, and 97, which survived every odd divisor she threw at it and came out prime, correctly, for the first time all afternoon. Then she entered 1000003 and the program chewed on it for a moment and said prime.

"That's the one Ms. Li will test," Gurshaan said. "She loves the big ones. She'll call it prestigious if it's fast."

"It's fast," Eleanor said. "It's doing half of what it did before and getting better answers."

Japji held up his hand toward his camera, and Eleanor held up hers toward his pixelated blur. Gurshaan, two screens away, did the same.

Eleanor saved the file, then entered one more number, 2, just to be sure. The program thought about the loneliest prime of all and printed its answer.

"Prime," she read aloud, and closed the laptop over a finally cold bowl of cereal.
